title: The record that was not yours
summary: Find an object-level authorization gap, design tests for ownership boundaries, and enforce access in code.

scenario.briefing: The billing API checks that a user is signed in, then loads an invoice by the id in the URL. A support account reported seeing another customer's invoice. Review the handler, choose the tests that would have caught it, and write the ownership check.

objectives.description: Identify the missing object-level authorization check.
Choose tests that exercise ownership boundaries.
Apply the same boundary to a new endpoint.

hints: Authentication answers who you are; authorization answers what this record allows.
The invoice id comes from the client, so the server must compare it with the session user.
Admin access should require an explicit permission, not merely the admin role.
Load the record, then allow the owner or an admin with billing:read; deny everyone else by default.

misconceptions.description: Believing a signed-in user may read any record by id.
misconceptions.feedback: Authentication does not grant access to every object. The handler must compare the record's owner with the session user.

misconceptions.description: Treating an unguessable identifier as an authorization control.
misconceptions.feedback: Ids leak through logs, links, and support tools. Randomness is not authorization; test the denial path explicitly.

misconceptions.description: Relying on a hidden button instead of a server check.
misconceptions.feedback: The client can issue any request it wants. Every object read or write needs a server-side ownership check.

misconceptions.description: Allowing access so the endpoint never returns a permission error.
misconceptions.feedback: An allow-by-default guard passes the owner case and every attack. Return false unless the owner or a scoped admin matches.

sections.title: Object-level authorization
sections.body: A route can require a valid session and still be wrong. Object-level authorization asks whether this user may act on this specific record. The check belongs next to the data access, where the record's owner is known.

sections.title: Deny by default
sections.body: Start from no access and add the owner case and any explicit, scoped override. An admin role without the billing permission is still a denial. A hidden button or an unguessable id changes nothing on the server.

sections.title: Test the negative path
sections.body: A test suite that only signs in as the owner cannot detect broken object-level authorization. Add a different user, an unauthenticated request, and an admin without the required permission.

vocabulary.definition: Insecure direct object reference: reaching another user's record by changing an identifier.
A check that a specific user may act on a specific record.
Refusing access unless an explicit rule allows it.
A permission that names the action and resource it covers.

steps.title: Review the invoice handler
steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.
hints: Trace how the invoice id enters the query.
Look for a comparison between the record owner and the session user.
Ask what the role check does and does not guarantee.
Reject the handler: it loads by client id and never checks ownership.

artifact.title: GET /api/invoices/:id
artifact.caption: The route requires a session but loads the record directly by path id.

findings.label: The invoice is loaded by the client-supplied path id.
The handler never compares the invoice owner with the session user.
Any signed-in non-guest user can change the id in the URL.
Admin access should require an explicit billing permission, not only the role name.
Rejecting guests is sufficient object-level authorization.

verdicts.label: Reject until ownership is checked per record
Add a log line and ship

steps.explanation: The session check only proves that someone is signed in. The handler must compare the invoice owner with the user, and any admin override needs a scoped permission.

steps.title: Choose the authorization tests
steps.prompt: Select the test cases you would keep for this endpoint.
hints: Include the allowed owner case so the endpoint still works.
Add a different signed-in user and an unauthenticated request.
Test an admin with and without the billing permission.
Keep owner, other user, guest, scoped admin, and unscoped admin; drop the idea that a UUID is a secret.

cases.label: Another customer reads the same id → 403
Admin with billing:read reads any invoice → 200
Checking that the id is a UUID is enough

steps.explanation: Authorization needs both the allow case and the denial cases. A UUID check validates shape, not permission.

steps.title: Write the ownership guard
steps.prompt: Edit access.js. canReadInvoice(user, invoice) returns true only for the invoice owner or an admin holding billing:read.
hints: Compare the user id with the invoice owner id first.
Return false when there is no user or no invoice.
An admin still needs the billing:read permission.
Use an explicit allow expression, then return false as the default.

steps.title: Apply the boundary to a new endpoint
steps.prompt: Select every accurate statement about object-level authorization.
hints: Think about what the server knows that the browser does not.
Separate authentication from authorization.
Consider what happens when the id is copied from a log or link.
Select server-side checks and deny-by-default; reject hidden UI and unguessable ids as controls.

statements.label: The server must check ownership for every record it returns or changes.
Starting from deny and adding explicit allow rules is safer than starting from allow.
An admin override should name the action and resource it covers.
Hiding the edit button in the client prevents unauthorized writes.
A random UUID is an authorization control because it cannot be guessed.

steps.explanation: Object-level authorization is a server-side decision. The client cannot be trusted to hide actions, and identifiers are not secrets.

accessibility.summary: The review, test selection, code editor, and explanation all use standard keyboard controls and text results.
accessibility.keyboardNotes: Use Tab to reach each finding, case, and statement. Space toggles a selection; Ctrl+Enter runs the code checks.
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: Findings and cases announce their selected state and result. Code tests announce the expected and actual values.
